sections.html:
Hamden is a New Haven County town directly north of the city of New Haven, nicknamed the Land of the Sleeping Giant. It covers about 33 square miles, almost all land, and the 2020 population was 61,169. It borders Cheshire and Wallingford to the north, North Haven to the east, New Haven to the south, and Woodbridge and Bethany to the west.

The southern end is built up and hard to tell from New Haven. The northern end, around Mount Carmel, is more rural and sits under the Sleeping Giant hill formation. Hamden is mainly a residential suburb, and more residents commute into New Haven than work inside Hamden. The population jumped from 8,611 in 1920 to 19,020 in 1930 and passed 41,000 by 1960, so many houses date from those building years.

Hamden grew as a set of village-like areas, and buyers usually search by those names:

  • Mount Carmel, home to Quinnipiac University and the Sleeping Giant hill
  • Whitneyville, built around the old Eli Whitney mill site and his workers' stone houses
  • Spring Glen, along Whitney Avenue
  • Centerville, the town center
  • Highwood, West Woods, Hamden Plains and Dunbar Hill
  • Pine Rock, Augerville, Beecher Heights, the Mix District and the State Street area on the east side

Whitneyville has an unusual past. Eli Whitney built stone houses for his employees there, believed to be the first employer-provided housing in the country. Houses from that era and the early twentieth century are part of the stock, and they bring the usual age-related repair questions.

sections.h2: Taxes: who to call and when
sections.html:
TaskWhereHours and contact
Pay or ask about real estate taxTax Office, main floor, Hamden Government Center, 2750 Dixwell AvenueMonday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., (203) 287-7140
Pay onlineTown websiteAny time
Drop-off paymentDrop box to the right of the main entranceAny time

Real estate tax bills come twice a year, in a summer cycle and a January cycle. Phone the Tax Office for the current due dates and the grace period, since the schedule has slipped before when the Legislative Council ran late on the budget. Cards are not taken at the counter.

On closing day, the title company asks the Tax Office what is still owed, and the unpaid balance is normally paid out of your sale proceeds.

The town and its school system, with 1,612 employees, are the largest employer, followed by Quinnipiac University at 850 to 900. Arden House, Whitney Center, CT Transit and AAA Hamden each employ a few hundred. No hospital sits inside the town limits, so residents use the large hospitals in New Haven. Retail, business services and manufacturing are the main local industries.

Quinnipiac has about 9,000 students on its Mount Carmel and York Hill campuses, which puts a lot of renters in town. If you own a small rental near campus and the tenant situation has become hard to manage, selling as is to a buyer who takes the property with the lease in place can spare you a turnover and cleanup before closing.

The Wilbur Cross Parkway runs through the middle of Hamden, toward Hartford one way and the New York area the other. Route 40, a spur expressway, links Mount Carmel to Interstate 91. Whitney Avenue is the main north-south road and Dixwell Avenue the main east-west road, and both carry Route 10 over part of their length.

CT Transit's New Haven division runs the Dixwell Avenue and Whitney Avenue bus routes, plus secondary routes on State Street, Winchester Avenue and Shelton Avenue. There is no rail station in town now, though a Hartford Line station is planned beside the Hamden and North Haven border near the Route 40 connector. Tweed New Haven in East Haven and Bradley International in Windsor Locks are the nearest commercial airports. The Farmington Canal Trail follows a canal route that boats used from 1825 to 1848.

About 5,398 students attend Hamden Public Schools, which cover elementary grades, a grade 7 and 8 middle school and Hamden High School. Wintergreen Magnet School and Eli Whitney Technical High School are in town too, along with Hamden Hall Country Day School and Sacred Heart Academy. Send enrollment questions to the school itself.

Utility providers are worth writing down for the buyer. Electricity comes from United Illuminating, gas from Southern Connecticut Gas, and water from the South Central Connecticut Regional Water Authority.

Recording a Hamden deed triggers a transfer charge that the town clerk collects. Section 12-494 of the General Statutes sets 0.75 percent for the state and 0.25 percent for the town on sales from $2,000 up.

Residential sales of $800,000 or more move into tiers. Non-residential property pays a state rate of 1.25 percent, and a town designated a targeted investment community may add up to another 0.25 percent. Chapter 223 on the General Assembly site has the wording. Your closing attorney can give the exact amount for your price, and it is paid from your proceeds, so subtract it before comparing offers.

If speed matters in Hamden, you have three paths. An agent can list the house, you can sell it yourself, or a buyer can pay cash and take the place untouched. Pick by asking how much work the house needs and how soon the keys must change hands.

  • Agent listing: widest audience, but repairs, cleaning and weeks of open houses come with it
  • Do-it-yourself sale: no commission, though you write the ad, field the calls and negotiate the contract
  • Cash purchase: usually fastest, few contingencies, no fix-up list, and a price that reflects those savings

Cash buyers show up most often for inherited homes, houses with tenants, and places with years of deferred upkeep. Get the offer on paper, pin down the closing date, and compare the net to what a listing might clear after commission and repairs.

Collect the deed, your latest tax bill, any mortgage payoff figure and, for a rental, the lease and tenant contact details. If the owner has died, bring the paperwork showing who is authorized to sign. In Hamden's older sections, such as Whitneyville and the early twentieth century streets, also gather records of any wiring, roof or heating work, since buyers ask for them.

A cash buyer typically walks the house, makes an offer in writing, and orders the title search. The closing attorney then prepares the deed and the conveyance tax return, pays off any tax or mortgage balance from your proceeds, and records the deed with the town clerk. Few steps wait on a lender, so the date mostly depends on how clean the title is. Tell the attorney early about liens, unpaid tax or a tenant who will stay.

faqs.q: What county is Hamden, CT in?
faqs.a: New Haven County. Hamden touches the city of New Haven along its southern edge.

faqs.q: How many people live in Hamden?
Where can I pay my Hamden property tax?
faqs.a: Pay online, mail a check, or visit the Tax Office at 2750 Dixwell Avenue between 8:30 a.m. and 4:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. The phone number is (203) 287-7140.
No. People here go to the big hospitals in New Haven.

faqs.q: What conveyance tax will I owe selling in Hamden?
faqs.a: The base under section 12-494 is 0.75 percent for the state and 0.25 percent for the town. Non-residential property and residential sales of $800,000 or more pay more, so ask your closing attorney for your exact figure.
